Probability & Statistics · Chapter 3

Chapter 3
Probability

Lectures 5–8 · the language of uncertainty, how to reason with it, and how it goes wrong

You use probability every day without calling it that. "70% chance of rain." "One in a billion chance of a random DNA match." "This email is probably spam." "If I take the express I'll probably make it." Each is a statement about something uncertain, and each guides a decision: take an umbrella, convict or acquit, delete the email, run for the train.

Chapter 1 drew the map of the course: probability reasons forwards, from a mechanism to the data it produces. Before we can reason backwards from data to mechanisms (inference), we need a precise language for uncertainty. This chapter builds it. The rules turn out to be few and simple. The trouble is that human intuition about probability is famously bad, and some of the mistakes it leads to have sent innocent people to prison. So alongside the rules, we'll keep meeting situations where your gut says one thing and the mathematics says another, and you'll learn to trust the mathematics.

Probability serves both of the course's goals, in opposite directions. Reasoning forwards, from a known mechanism to the data it will produce, is prediction: if a test is 90% sensitive, gives false alarms for 9% of healthy people, and the disease affects 1% of people, how many positive tests should a clinic expect? Reasoning backwards, from observed data to the mechanism that produced them, is inference: given that this patient tested positive, how likely is it that she has the disease? Most of this chapter builds the forward machinery; Section 3.6 then shows how Bayes' theorem runs it in reverse, and that reversal is the seed from which all of statistical inference grows.

Here is the route through the chapter.

  • Sections 3.1 to 3.3 set up the language: what a probability means, how to describe events as sets, and the three rules every probability must obey.
  • Section 3.4 turns probability into counting, for situations where every outcome is equally likely.
  • Sections 3.5 and 3.6 are the heart of the chapter: how probabilities change when we learn something (conditional probability), how to translate a word problem into symbols, and how to reason backwards from evidence to causes (Bayes' theorem).
  • Section 3.7 shows how to let a computer do the work by simulation.
  • Section 3.8 attaches numbers to outcomes, which sets up the next two chapters.

Think About It: Test Your Intuition First

Before reading on, write down quick answers to these three questions. Don't calculate; just guess. You'll meet each one properly later in the chapter, and it's worth knowing how good your intuition is before you start.

  1. How many people do you need in a room for it to be more likely than not that two of them share a birthday?
  2. A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test for it is 90% accurate for people who have it, and gives false alarms for only 9% of people who don't. You test positive. Roughly how likely is it that you have the disease?
  3. On a game show you pick one of three doors; the host, who knows where the prize is, opens another door to show it's empty, and offers you a switch. Does switching help?

The answers are 23 people (Example 3.9), about 9% (Example 3.18), and yes: switching doubles your chance (Example 3.21). If you got all three right without having seen them before, you're very unusual. Most people, including most doctors for question 2, get them badly wrong. That's not a failing of intelligence; it's a sign that probability needs to be calculated, not felt.

3.1 What does probability mean?

Three ways to read a probability

What does it mean to say a coin lands heads with probability 12? People have given three different answers.

  1. Equally likely outcomes (classical). There are two faces and nothing to favour either, so each gets half. This works for coins, dice and lotteries, where symmetry tells us the outcomes are equally likely. It doesn't tell us the probability that a drug works or that it rains.
  2. Long-run frequency (frequentist). Flip the coin many, many times: the fraction of heads settles down to 12. A probability is the fraction of the time something happens in a long run of repetitions. This is how a casino, an insurer, or a lab estimating a test's error rate thinks.
  3. Degree of belief (Bayesian). A probability measures how strongly a reasonable person should believe something, given what they know. This makes sense even for one-off events: "the probability that this suspect left this fingerprint", "the probability that this vaccine works".

The three interpretations disagree about what probability is, but they agree on the rules probability must follow. That's what makes probability so useful: the same rules serve the casino, the scientist and the juror.

Here is the long-run idea in action. Toss a coin over and over, and track the fraction of heads.

Watch the Law of Large Numbers happen

Set the true probability of heads, then toss. The line tracks the running proportion of heads after each toss; the dashed line is the true probability. Early on the line jumps around. With many tosses it settles down. Press new run a few times and compare how different the early paths are.

Early on the fraction swings wildly; after hundreds of tosses it barely moves. This settling-down is called the Law of Large Numbers. We'll state it precisely and prove it in Chapter 7; for now, it justifies estimating a probability by a long-run fraction.

Definition: Probability as Long-Run Frequency (Informal)

If an experiment can be repeated independently under the same conditions, the probability of an event is the value that the fraction of repetitions in which the event occurs settles down to as the number of repetitions grows.

Example 3.1: Rolling a Die by Computer ★ lecture example

A fair die has six equally likely faces, so the classical probability of rolling a six is 16≈0.167. Use R to roll a die 10, 100, 1,000 and 100,000 times, and compare the fraction of sixes with 16.

sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE) rolls a fair die n times: it draws from the numbers 1 to 6, putting each one back before the next draw. Comparing with == 6 gives TRUE for each six, and mean() of a TRUE/FALSE vector is the fraction of TRUEs.

R
set.seed(3)
for (n in c(10, 100, 1000, 100000)) {
  rolls <- sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE)
  cat(format(n, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), "rolls: fraction of sixes =", mean(rolls == 6), "\n")
}
output
10 rolls: fraction of sixes = 0 
100 rolls: fraction of sixes = 0.15 
1,000 rolls: fraction of sixes = 0.174 
100,000 rolls: fraction of sixes = 0.16699

With 10 rolls the fraction can be far from 16. With 100,000 rolls it's within a fraction of a percentage point. Notice that the error shrinks as n grows, but not in proportion: 100 times as many rolls doesn't make the error 100 times smaller. Chapter 7 shows that it shrinks roughly like 1/n, so 100 times the data buys about 10 times the precision.

A plot of the running fraction of sixes in one long sequence of rolls shows the settling-down directly. The horizontal axis is on a log scale, so that early and late rolls both show up:

R
set.seed(6)
rolls <- sample(1:6, 10000, replace = TRUE)
running <- cumsum(rolls == 6) / seq_along(rolls)
ggplot(data.frame(n = seq_along(rolls), running), aes(n, running)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1/6, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "number of rolls (log scale)", y = "fraction of sixes")

Empirical probability: probabilities from data

For a die we know the probability in advance. Most of the time we don't. What is the probability that a randomly chosen eruption of Old Faithful lasts more than 3 minutes? That a hospital patient with these symptoms needs intensive care? That a new email is spam? Nobody can work these out from symmetry. Instead, we look at what happened in the past and count.

Definition: Empirical Probability

Suppose an experiment has been observed n times, and event A happened in nA of them. The empirical probability (or relative frequency) of A is Pr̂(A)=nAn=number of times A happenednumber of observations. The "hat" on Pr̂ is a reminder that this is an estimate of the true probability Pr(A), computed from data.

The Law of Large Numbers is what makes empirical probabilities worth computing: if the observations are independent repetitions of the same experiment, then as n grows, Pr̂(A) settles down to the true Pr(A). The empirical probability is the statistic; the true probability is the parameter (Section 1.3).

Example 3.2: Estimating a Probability from Old Faithful ★ lecture example

Using the 272 eruptions in faithful, estimate the probability that an eruption lasts more than 3 minutes. How much would your estimate have differed if you had only seen the first 20 eruptions? Plot the estimate as the eruptions accumulate.

Reading the problem. The "experiment" is one eruption. The event is A = "lasts more than 3 minutes". We count how many of the 272 eruptions are in A.

R
e <- faithful$eruptions
sum(e > 3)              # n_A: eruptions longer than 3 minutes
length(e)               # n
mean(e > 3)             # empirical probability n_A / n
mean(e[1:20] > 3)       # using only the first 20 eruptions
output
[1] 175
[1] 272
[1] 0.6433824
[1] 0.55

So Pr̂(longer than 3 minutes)=175272≈0.643. From the first 20 eruptions alone, the estimate would have been 11/20=0.55, quite a bit lower. To see how the estimate settles down, compute it after each new eruption: the running fraction after k eruptions is the number of long eruptions among the first k, divided by k. R's cumsum() gives running totals:

R
running <- cumsum(e > 3) / seq_along(e)
ggplot(data.frame(k = seq_along(e), running), aes(k, running)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(e > 3), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "number of eruptions observed", y = "fraction over 3 min")

This is the Law of Large Numbers on real data: early estimates jump about, later ones barely move.

A critical caveat. The Law of Large Numbers needs independent repetitions of the same experiment. Eruptions are not quite independent (a long eruption tends to follow a short one, as you can check with table(head(e > 3, -1), tail(e > 3, -1))), and the geyser's behaviour changes slowly over the years. So 0.643 estimates the probability for Old Faithful during the period these data were collected. An empirical probability is only as good as the assumption that the future works like the past (Chapter 1's chicken).

Example 3.3: What Does "70% Chance of Rain" Mean?

A weather forecast says there is a 70% chance of rain in Manhattan tomorrow. Explain what this means in long-run terms, and how you could check whether a forecaster's probabilities can be trusted.

Tomorrow happens only once, so we can't repeat it. But we can look at all the days on which this forecaster said "70%", and compute the empirical probability of rain on those days. If the forecasts are good, it should have rained on about 70% of them, on about 30% of the days they said "30%", and so on. A forecaster whose probabilities pass this test is called well calibrated.

US National Weather Service forecasts are well calibrated in this sense, and checking calibration is exactly how forecasting services (and, these days, machine learning models) are evaluated. Note what a 70% forecast does not mean: it doesn't mean it will rain for 70% of the day, or over 70% of the city.

Bayesian Inference: Probability as a Betting Price

How can a belief be a number? The Bayesian answer: your probability for an event is the price you would consider fair for a ticket that pays $1 if the event happens. If you'd pay 70¢ for a "rain tomorrow" ticket, your probability is 0.7.

This simple idea forces beliefs to obey the rules of probability. Suppose you price "rain" at 70¢ and "no rain" at 50¢. Someone sells you both tickets for $1.20. Whatever the weather, exactly one ticket pays out, so you get back $1 and lose 20¢ for certain. A set of prices that lets someone make a guaranteed profit off you is called a Dutch book, and the only way to avoid one is to make your prices follow the rules in Section 3.3. Rational beliefs, it turns out, must be probabilities.

History: A Gambler's Question

Probability theory was born in 1654 from a gambling problem. A French writer and gambler, the Chevalier de Méré, asked the mathematician Blaise Pascal a question about dice (we'll answer it in Example 3.15), and a second one, the problem of points: how should the pot be divided fairly if a game is stopped before anyone has won? Pascal wrote to Pierre de Fermat, and in a famous exchange of letters the two solved it, laying the foundations of the subject. Earlier, the Italian physician and gambler Gerolamo Cardano had written a book on games of chance in the 1560s, though it wasn't published until 1663.

Check Yourself

There aren't four symmetric outcomes, and this one patient can't be treated over and over. Which reading still makes sense for a one-off event?

It's a statement about one patient, so it is most naturally a degree of belief, informed by data on similar patients. (A frequentist would rephrase it: "among patients like this one, about 25% respond", an empirical probability.)

degree of belief

A lab re-tests 400 samples that were originally reported positive and finds that 100 of them were false positives. What is the empirical probability that a reported positive is false?

Count the times the event happened and divide by the number of observations.

Pr̂(false)=100/400=0.25. It is an estimate: another 400 samples would give a somewhat different fraction.

You flip a fair coin 10 times and get 7 heads. Which statement is correct?

Does the coin remember what it did? This belief has a name: the gambler's fallacy.

Suppose the next 990 flips come out exactly half heads. Is the excess of heads gone, or just small compared with the total?

The coin has no memory. After 10 flips with 7 heads, if the next 990 are exactly half heads you'd have 502 heads in 1,000: still 2 extra heads, but the fraction is 0.502. The fraction settles down because the early excess is swamped, not corrected.

Think About It: Can the Future Be Estimated from the Past?

An insurance company has 50 years of data showing that 0.3% of homes in a county flood each year, and prices its policies on that empirical probability. List two reasons the next 50 years might not behave like the last 50. What does this say about using empirical probabilities to predict?

The mechanism may change: a warming climate brings heavier rainfall and rising seas, and new building in the floodplain changes how water drains. The data may also be unrepresentative: 50 years is short for rare events, so a single unusually wet or dry decade can distort the estimate. An empirical probability is a good prediction only if the process that generated the past data keeps working the same way (Chapter 1's chicken). Insurers increasingly combine past data with models of the mechanism (climate and hydrology) for exactly this reason: inference about the mechanism makes for better prediction.

Key Takeaways

  • Probability can be read as symmetry, as a long-run frequency, or as a degree of belief. All three follow the same rules.
  • The empirical probability Pr̂(A)=nA/n estimates Pr(A) from data.
  • The Law of Large Numbers: in many independent repetitions, the fraction of times an event happens settles down to its probability. The error shrinks roughly like 1/n.
  • Empirical probabilities assume the future works like the past.

3.2 Experiments, outcomes and events

To reason precisely we need a vocabulary. Any process with an uncertain result, from rolling a die to running a DNA test, is called an experiment.

Definition: Sample Space and Events

  • The sample space S of an experiment is the set of all its possible outcomes.
  • An event is a set of outcomes, that is, a subset of S. An event occurs if the outcome of the experiment is one of its members.

Some examples:

  • A drug screen returns negative, inconclusive or positive: S={neg,inc,pos}. The event "not negative" is {inc,pos}.
  • We count failed login attempts on a server in one hour: S={0,1,2,…}. The event "more than 5 attempts" is {6,7,8,…}.
  • We measure the time, in hours, until a lab centrifuge fails: S=[0,∞). The event "it lasts at least 1,000 hours" is the interval [1000,∞).

Why bother with sets? Because it turns vague questions into precise ones. "What's the chance the test isn't negative?" becomes "what's the probability of the set {inc,pos}?", and sets can be combined, compared and counted.

Combining events

Events are sets, so we combine them with set operations. In words and in symbols:

Definition: Combining Events

For events A and B in a sample space S:

  • A or B (the union) A∪B: the outcomes in A, in B, or in both.
  • A and B (the intersection) A∩B: the outcomes in both A and B.
  • not A (the complement) Ac: the outcomes in S that are not in A.
  • A and B are disjoint (or mutually exclusive) if they can't both happen: A∩B=⌀, where ⌀ is the empty set, the event containing no outcomes.
  • A is a subset of B, written A⊆B, if every outcome in A is also in B: whenever A happens, B happens.

In mathematics, "or" always means "one or the other or both." Venn diagrams make these operations visible: draw S as a rectangle and events as regions inside it. The shaded outcomes belong to the event.

Some combinations are built from these: "A but not B" is A∩Bc, and "exactly one of A and B" is (A∩Bc)∪(Ac∩B). The best way to get fluent is to practise in both directions: from a picture to symbols, and from symbols to a picture.

Click the regions, read the set

The rectangle is the sample space S and the circles are events. Click any region (or use the buttons below the picture) to shade it, and the readout gives the event you have shaded in set notation and in words. Then try a challenge: choose an event from the list and shade exactly that event.

Theorem: De Morgan's Laws

For any events A and B, (A∪B)c=Ac∩Bcand(A∩B)c=Ac∪Bc. In words: "not (A or B)" is "neither A nor B"; "not (A and B)" is "not A, or not B (or both)".

First law. We show the two sets contain exactly the same outcomes. An outcome is in (A∪B)c exactly when it is not in A∪B. That means it is in neither A nor B: it is not in A (so it's in Ac) and not in B (so it's in Bc). So it is in Ac∩Bc. Every step can be read backwards, so the two sets are equal.

Second law. Apply the first law to the events Ac and Bc (whose complements are A and B): (Ac∪Bc)c=A∩B. Taking the complement of both sides gives Ac∪Bc=(A∩B)c. ◼∎

You can check De Morgan's laws in the widget: shade "neither" in the two-event diagram, and the readout offers both ways of writing it.

Example 3.4: Describing Events at a Login Server

A server records, for each login attempt, whether the password was correct (P) and whether the attempt came from a new device (N). Write each event in symbols:

  1. The password was wrong.
  2. The password was correct and the device was new.
  3. At least one warning sign: a wrong password or a new device.
  4. No warning signs.

Strategy. Translate each phrase piece by piece: "wrong password" is "not P"; "and" is ∩; "or" (and "at least one") is ∪; "no ... at all" is the complement of "at least one".

  1. Pc.
  2. P∩N.
  3. The two warning signs are Pc and N, so "at least one" is Pc∪N.
  4. Neither warning sign: the password was correct and the device was not new, P∩Nc. By De Morgan this is (Pc∪N)c, the complement of part 3, as it should be: "no warning signs" is the opposite of "at least one warning sign".

Check Yourself

A forensic lab tests a fingerprint (F = "a usable print was recovered") and a DNA swab (D = "a usable DNA profile was recovered").

"At least one" means one or the other or both. Which set operation means that?

F∪D: the print, the DNA, or both.

F∪D

"No evidence" means no usable print and no usable DNA. Then compare with De Morgan's laws.

Fc∩Dc, which by De Morgan equals (F∪D)c: the complement of "at least one". Note Fc∪Dc is different: it means "at least one test failed".

Fc∩Dc

"But" means "and". Which event is required, and which is ruled out?

F∩Dc: in F, and not in D. Shade it in the two-event widget to check.

F∩Dc

Think About It: Defining the Event Is Half the Battle

A news report says "the chance of a major earthquake in the region is 70%". Before you can judge or use that number, what must you know about the event? List at least three things the sentence leaves out.

What counts as "major" (magnitude 6.7? 7?); over what time period (next year? next 30 years?); and what region exactly (a city? a whole state?). The probability of an event depends entirely on how the event is defined: "at least one magnitude-6.7 earthquake in the San Francisco Bay Area in the next 30 years" is a precise set of outcomes; "a major earthquake in the region" is not. (The US Geological Survey's widely quoted estimate is of the precise form.) Precise events are the first step to useful predictions.

Key Takeaways

  • The sample space lists every possible outcome; an event is a set of outcomes.
  • Union = or (inclusive), intersection = and, complement = not. Disjoint events can't happen together.
  • De Morgan: not(A or B) = (not A) and (not B); not(A and B) = (not A) or (not B).

3.3 The rules of probability

What rules should any sensible assignment of probabilities follow? Think about long-run fractions, or empirical probabilities. A fraction of the time is never negative and never more than 1. Something certain to happen happens 100% of the time. And if two events can't happen together, the fraction of times that one or the other happens is the sum of their fractions. Remarkably, these three properties are all we need.

Definition: The Axioms of Probability (Kolmogorov)

A probability on a sample space S assigns to each event A a number Pr(A) such that:

  1. Pr(A)≥0 for every event A;
  2. Pr(S)=1;
  3. if A1,A2,A3,… are events no two of which can happen together (pairwise disjoint), then Pr(A1∪A2∪A3∪⋯)=Pr(A1)+Pr(A2)+Pr(A3)+⋯.

Everything else follows from these. Here are the consequences you'll use constantly.

Theorem: Consequences of the Axioms

For any events A and B:

  1. Complement rule. Pr(Ac)=1−Pr(A).
  2. The impossible event. Pr(⌀)=0.
  3. Bounds. 0≤Pr(A)≤1, and if A⊆B (whenever A happens, so does B) then Pr(A)≤Pr(B).
  4. Addition rule. Pr(A∪B)=Pr(A)+Pr(B)−Pr(A∩B).
  5. Union bound. Pr(A∪B)≤Pr(A)+Pr(B).

We prove 2 first. S=S∪⌀∪⌀∪⋯, and these sets are pairwise disjoint, so axiom 3 gives Pr(S)=Pr(S)+Pr(⌀)+Pr(⌀)+⋯. This is only possible if Pr(⌀)=0. As a bonus, axiom 3 now works for finitely many disjoint events too: pad the list with copies of ⌀, which add nothing.

  1. A and Ac are disjoint and together make up S. By axiom 3 (for two events) and axiom 2, Pr(A)+Pr(Ac)=Pr(S)=1. Subtract Pr(A).

  2. Shown above.

  3. If A⊆B, split B into the disjoint pieces A and B∩Ac. Then Pr(B)=Pr(A)+Pr(B∩Ac)≥Pr(A), by axiom 1. Taking B=S gives Pr(A)≤1.

  4. Split A∪B into three disjoint pieces: only A (A∩Bc), both (A∩B), and only B (Ac∩B). Then Pr(A∪B)=Pr(A∩Bc)+Pr(A∩B)+Pr(Ac∩B),Pr(A)=Pr(A∩Bc)+Pr(A∩B),Pr(B)=Pr(Ac∩B)+Pr(A∩B).Pr(A∪B)=Pr(A∩Bc)+Pr(A∩B)+Pr(Ac∩B),Pr(A)=Pr(A∩Bc)+Pr(A∩B),Pr(B)=Pr(Ac∩B)+Pr(A∩B). Adding the last two lines counts the middle piece Pr(A∩B) twice, so Pr(A)+Pr(B)=Pr(A∪B)+Pr(A∩B). Rearrange.

  5. From 4, because Pr(A∩B)≥0. ◼∎

The addition rule is easiest to see in a picture. Move the sliders, and watch which areas get counted twice.

Two events, one picture

Set the probabilities of two events A and B and of their overlap. The areas in the diagram are drawn to scale inside a square of total area 1. The readout applies the rules of this chapter: complements, the addition rule, conditional probability, and a check for independence. Try making the overlap equal to Pr(A) × Pr(B), and try making it zero.

Example 3.5: Women or Children on the Titanic ★ lecture example

When the RMS Titanic sank in April 1912, about 2,200 people were aboard. A British inquiry recorded each person's class, sex, age group and whether they survived; R's Titanic dataset contains those counts (as compiled by R. Dawson, Journal of Statistics Education, 1995). Pick one person aboard at random. What is the probability that the person was female or a child?

Reading the problem. "Pick at random" makes every person equally likely, so a probability is a count divided by the 2,201 people aboard. Name the events: F = female, C = child. The question asks for Pr(F∪C) ("or").

First the counts of sex by age group:

R
tt <- as.data.frame(Titanic)                 # one row per combination, with a count
xtabs(Freq ~ Sex + Age, data = tt)           # cross-tabulate sex by age
output
        Age
Sex      Child Adult
  Male      64  1667
  Female    45   425

There were 45+425=470 females, 64+45=109 children, and 45 girls, who are both. The addition rule gives Pr(F∪C)=Pr(F)+Pr(C)−Pr(F∩C)=4702201+1092201−452201=5342201≈0.243.Pr(F∪C)=Pr(F)+Pr(C)−Pr(F∩C)=4702201+1092201−452201=5342201≈0.243. Simply adding 470 and 109 would count the 45 girls twice. The answer is 534 people: about 24% of everyone aboard, the group a "women and children first" policy was meant to protect.

Example 3.6: At Least One Alarm

A company's network has two intrusion detectors. Over the past year, detector A raised a false alarm on 3% of days, detector B on 4% of days, and both on 1% of days.

  1. On what fraction of days did at least one detector raise a false alarm?
  2. On what fraction of days did neither?
  3. Without knowing the 1% figure, what can you say for certain about part 1?

Reading the problem. Let A and B be the events that detectors A and B falsely alarm on a given day. Then Pr(A)=0.03, Pr(B)=0.04, Pr(A∩B)=0.01 ("both"). "At least one" is A∪B; "neither" is its complement.

  1. Addition rule: Pr(A∪B)=0.03+0.04−0.01=0.06.
  2. Complement rule: Pr((A∪B)c)=1−0.06=0.94.
  3. The union bound gives Pr(A∪B)≤0.03+0.04=0.07, whatever the overlap.

Notice the detectors are far from independent (Section 3.5): if they were, both would alarm on only 0.03×0.04=0.12% of days, not 1%. They probably react to the same unusual traffic. Security teams use the union bound constantly: with 50 detectors each falsely alarming on 1% of days, the chance of at least one false alarm on a given day could be as large as 50%. More alarms means more false alarms.

Check Yourself

In a city, 30% of burglaries involve forced entry, 20% happen at night, and 10% involve forced entry at night.

What is the probability that a randomly chosen burglary involves forced entry or happens at night (or both)?

Add the two probabilities, then remove what you counted twice.

0.3+0.2−0.1=0.4.

What is the probability that it involves neither?

"Neither" is the complement of "one or the other or both".

1−0.4=0.6.

What is the probability that it involves forced entry but did not happen at night?

Forced entry splits into "forced and night" and "forced and not night". You know the total and one piece.

Pr(F∩Nc)=Pr(F)−Pr(F∩N)=0.3−0.1=0.2.

Interlude (Optional): Probability as Measurement

The axioms look abstract, but they are the same rules obeyed by every way we measure the size of things. Length, area, volume, mass and probability all assign a non-negative number to a region, and all are additive: the size of two non-overlapping pieces is the sum of their sizes. Mathematicians call any such rule a measure, and probability is simply a measure whose total is 1.

Picture throwing a dart at a square board, landing uniformly at random. The probability it lands in a region is that region's share of the area. This also explains something puzzling. The chance the dart hits one exact point, say the dead centre, is zero, because a point has no area. Yet the dart lands somewhere, on a point that had probability zero. So probability zero doesn't mean impossible. This happens whenever outcomes are measurements (times, weights, concentrations), and it's why Chapter 5 works with areas under curves instead of probabilities of single values.

There is a deeper surprise. In 1905 Giuseppe Vitali showed that it is impossible to assign a sensible "length" to every subset of a line; and in 1924 Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski showed that a solid ball can be cut into finitely many pieces (five turn out to be enough) and reassembled into two balls the same size as the first. The pieces are so strange they have no volume at all. The fix is to measure only well-behaved sets, called measurable sets. When Andrey Kolmogorov wrote down the axioms of probability in 1933, he built them on exactly this theory of measure, and every probability course since stands on his foundation. You will never meet an unmeasurable event in practice, but it's worth knowing that even "how big is this set?" turned out to have a subtle answer.

Why it matters: every rule in this chapter is a rule about measuring sizes, which is why Venn-diagram areas are such a faithful picture of probability.

Think About It: Do the Probabilities Add Up?

A sports commentator says: "Team A has a 60% chance of winning the league, Team B has 30%, and Team C has 25%." What's wrong? If you trusted the commentator's numbers, how could someone take advantage of you?

The three teams can't all win, so the events are disjoint, and their probabilities should add to at most 1; here they add to 1.15. By the Dutch book argument (Section 3.1), someone could sell you a $1 ticket on each team at those prices: you'd pay $1.15 and collect exactly $1 whichever team wins (or less, if a fourth team wins), losing at least 15 cents for certain. Probabilities that break the axioms are not just untidy; they lead to bad decisions.

Key Takeaways

  • Three axioms: probabilities are non-negative, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of disjoint events add.
  • Complement rule Pr(Ac)=1−Pr(A). Addition rule Pr(A∪B)=Pr(A)+Pr(B)−Pr(A∩B).
  • "At least one" problems are often easiest through the complement: 1−Pr(none).

3.4 Equally likely outcomes and counting

When all outcomes in a finite sample space are equally likely (fair dice, shuffled cards, random samples, random passwords), the axioms give a simple formula.

Theorem: Equally Likely Outcomes

If S has N outcomes, all equally likely, then for any event A containing nA outcomes, Pr(A)=nAN. In words: the number of outcomes in A divided by the number of outcomes in S.

The N single outcomes are disjoint and together make up S, so by axioms 2 and 3 their equal probabilities add to 1: each has probability 1/N. The event A is the disjoint union of its nA outcomes, so Pr(A)=nA×1N. ◼∎

So probability becomes counting. The trouble is that the counts are often astronomically large: nobody can list all the possible poker hands, let alone all the possible 8-character passwords. We need shortcuts, and they all grow from one idea.

The multiplication rule

Theorem: Multiplication Rule for Counting

If a task is done in k stages, with n1 ways to do stage 1, then n2 ways to do stage 2 (whatever happened in stage 1), and so on, the whole task can be done in n1×n2×⋯×nk ways.

Picture a tree: n1 branches for stage 1, each splitting into n2 branches for stage 2, and so on. Each complete path from the root to a leaf is one way of doing the whole task. After stage 1 there are n1 partial paths; each splits into n2, giving n1n2 after stage 2; and so on. After k stages there are n1n2⋯nk paths. ◼∎

For example, a meal deal with 3 mains, 4 sides and 2 drinks gives 3×4×2=24 different meals.

The four ways to choose

Most counting problems ask: in how many ways can we choose k items from n distinct items? The answer depends on two questions, which you should ask every time:

  1. Does order matter? Is "Alice then Bob" different from "Bob then Alice"? For a race (gold, silver), yes; for a committee, no.
  2. Is replacement allowed? Can the same item be chosen more than once? For the digits of a PIN, yes; for people on a committee, no.

Two yes/no questions give four cases. We take them one at a time, each with a motivating example, a formula and a proof.

with replacement (repeats allowed) without replacement (no repeats)
order matters nk n!(n−k)!
order doesn't matter (n+k−1k) (nk)=n!k!(n−k)!

Here n!=n×(n−1)×⋯×2×1 ("n factorial"), with the convention 0!=1. In R: factorial(n) and choose(n, k).

Case 1: order matters, with replacement

A PIN has 4 digits, each from 0 to 9, and digits can repeat. There are 10 choices for the first digit, 10 for the second, and so on: 104=10,000 PINs.

Theorem: Ordered Selections with Replacement

The number of ordered sequences of length k whose entries are each chosen from n distinct items, repeats allowed, is nk.

Each of the k positions is a stage with n choices, whatever was chosen before. By the multiplication rule, there are n×n×⋯×n=nk sequences. ◼∎

Example 3.7: How Long to Crack a Password? ★ lecture example

An attacker who has stolen a database of hashed passwords can test guesses offline. Assume a powerful attacker can test 10 billion (1010) guesses per second. How long does it take to try every possible password of length 8 if passwords use:

  1. lowercase letters only (26 symbols)?
  2. upper- and lowercase letters and digits (62 symbols)?
  3. all 94 printable keyboard characters?

Which case? A password is a sequence (order matters: "abc" and "cba" are different passwords) and characters can repeat ("aaa" is allowed). So with m symbols in each of 8 positions there are m8 passwords. Dividing by 1010 guesses per second gives the time in seconds.

R
m <- c(26, 62, 94)
n_passwords <- m^8
seconds <- n_passwords / 1e10
data.frame(symbols = m, passwords = signif(n_passwords, 3),
           hours = round(seconds / 3600, 3), days = round(seconds / 86400, 2))
output
  symbols passwords   hours days
1      26  2.09e+11   0.006 0.00
2      62  2.18e+14   6.065 0.25
3      94  6.10e+15 169.325 7.06
  1. 268≈2.1×1011 passwords: about 21 seconds.
  2. 628≈2.2×1014: about 6 hours.
  3. 948≈6.1×1015: about 7 days.

The numbers grow so fast that a picture needs a logarithmic axis, on which each gridline is 10 times the one below:

R
len <- 4:14
grid <- expand.grid(length = len, symbols = factor(c(26, 62, 94)))
grid$seconds <- as.numeric(as.character(grid$symbols))^grid$length / 1e10
ggplot(grid, aes(length, seconds, linetype = symbols)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = 10^c(-6, 0, 6, 12, 18), labels = scales::math_format(10^.x)(c(-6, 0, 6, 12, 18))) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(86400, 3.15e9), colour = "grey60") +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = c(86400, 3.15e9) * 6, label = c("1 day", "1 century"), hjust = 0, vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "password length", y = "seconds (log scale)",
       linetype = "symbols")

(The grey lines mark one day and one century.) Each extra character multiplies the work by m, which is why the lines are straight on a log scale. A 12-character password from 94 symbols would take about 1.5 million years. Length matters more than cleverness.

One caveat to think about: these counts assume every password is equally likely. Real people choose Password1! far more often than q7#Lr2!x, so attackers try common passwords first. "Equally likely" is a model, and here it flatters the defender.

Case 2: order matters, without replacement

Eight runners compete for gold, silver and bronze. Any of the 8 can win gold; once gold is decided, any of the remaining 7 can win silver; then any of the remaining 6, bronze: 8×7×6=336 possible podiums. Each choice uses up one runner, so the number of options falls by one at each stage.

Theorem: Ordered Selections Without Replacement (Permutations)

The number of ordered sequences of k different items chosen from n distinct items is n×(n−1)×⋯×(n−k+1)=n!(n−k)!. In particular, all n items can be arranged in n! orders.

Use the multiplication rule: n choices for the first position, then n−1 for the second (one item is used up), down to n−(k−1)=n−k+1 for the kth. For the second form, multiply and divide by (n−k)!=(n−k)(n−k−1)⋯1. The numerator becomes n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)×(n−k)⋯1=n!, so the product equals n!(n−k)!. With k=n, this is n!/0!=n!. ◼∎

Factorials grow astonishingly fast. A deck of 52 cards can be shuffled into 52!≈8×1067 orders, more than the number of atoms in the Earth, so every thorough shuffle you make has almost certainly never happened before.

Example 3.8: A Line-Up

A witness is shown a line-up of 6 people, one of whom is the suspect. If the 6 are arranged in a random order, what is the probability that the suspect stands in position 1? In positions 1, 2 or 3?

Which case? An arrangement is an ordering of all 6 people, without repeats: 6!=720 equally likely line-ups.

Position 1. Count the line-ups with the suspect first: the other 5 people can be arranged in the remaining 5 positions in 5!=120 ways. So Pr(suspect in position 1)=120720=16. That makes sense: by symmetry, the suspect is equally likely to be in any of the 6 positions.

Positions 1 to 3. The events "in position 1", "in position 2" and "in position 3" are disjoint, each with probability 16, so by axiom 3 the probability is 36=12.

R
factorial(6)
factorial(5) / factorial(6)
output
[1] 720
[1] 0.1666667

Random ordering matters in practice: witnesses tend to pick people in some positions more than others, and a fair procedure must not let the suspect's position give anything away.

Example 3.9: The Birthday Problem ★ lecture example

There are 23 people in a room. Assuming each is equally likely to have been born on any of 365 days (ignore 29 February), independently of the others, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday? Try the widget below first, after writing down your guess.

Strategy. "At least two share" is complicated: one pair, two pairs, three people with the same birthday... Its complement, "all 23 birthdays are different", is much simpler. So we find that and subtract from 1.

Count with cases 1 and 2. Write down the birthdays as a list in order (person 1's birthday, person 2's, and so on).

  • All possible lists: each of the 23 people has 365 possible birthdays, repeats allowed (case 1): 36523 equally likely lists.
  • Lists with no repeats: 365 choices for person 1, 364 for person 2, ..., down to 365−22=343 for person 23 (case 2): 365×364×⋯×343.

So Pr(all different)=365×364×⋯×34336523≈0.493, and Pr(at least one shared birthday)=1−0.493=0.507. With just 23 people, a match is more likely than not.

R
1 - prod(365:343) / 365^23      # by the formula
pbirthday(23)                   # R has a built-in function
output
[1] 0.5072972
[1] 0.5072972
R
people <- 1:80
p_match <- sapply(people, pbirthday)
ggplot(data.frame(people, p_match), aes(people, p_match)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "number of people", y = "Pr(shared birthday)")

Why does intuition fail so badly? We think about our own birthday, and the chance someone else shares it is small: 1−(364/365)22≈0.06 with 22 others. But the question is about any pair, and 23 people make (232)=253 pairs (case 3, below). Coincidences are much more common than they feel, which matters whenever someone says "what are the odds?" about a match in a large database.

The birthday problem

How many people must be in a room before it's more likely than not that two share a birthday? Before you touch anything, write down your guess. Then choose a room size and gather rooms of random people (365 equally likely birthdays, ignoring 29 February). The calendar shows the latest room: a red square is a birthday shared by two or more people. The curve below is the exact probability, which you'll be able to compute by the end of Section 3.4.

Case 3: order doesn't matter, without replacement

A lab must choose 2 of its 5 analysts to review a case. Ordered pairs (first reviewer, second reviewer) number 5×4=20 by case 2. But a review panel of Ana and Ben is the same panel as Ben and Ana: each panel was counted twice, once in each order. So there are 20/2=10 panels. The same idea, dividing out the orderings, works in general.

Theorem: Unordered Selections Without Replacement (Combinations)

The number of ways to choose k items from n distinct items, without repeats and when order doesn't matter, is (nk)=n!k!(n−k)!, read "n choose k". It is also the number of subsets of size k of a set of size n.

Count the ordered selections of k items in two ways.

  • Directly, by case 2: there are n!(n−k)! of them.
  • In two stages: first choose which k items (an unordered selection: (nk) ways, the number we want), then put those k items in order (k! ways, by case 2 with k=n). By the multiplication rule there are (nk)×k! ordered selections.

Both count the same thing, so (nk)×k!=n!(n−k)!⇒(nk)=n!k!(n−k)!.◼∎

Two quick checks: (n0)=(nn)=1 (one way to choose nothing, one way to choose everything), and (nk)=(nn−k) (choosing which k to take is the same as choosing which n−k to leave). Combinations are the most important counting tool in the course: Chapter 4's binomial distribution is built on them.

Example 3.10: The Powerball Jackpot

To win the US Powerball jackpot you must match 5 white balls drawn from 69 (order doesn't matter) and 1 red Powerball drawn from 26. What is the probability that one ticket wins?

Which cases? The white balls are drawn without replacement, and the order they come out doesn't matter: case 3, (695) ways. The red ball can be any of 26. By the multiplication rule there are (695)×26 equally likely outcomes, and one ticket matches exactly one of them.

R
choose(69, 5)
choose(69, 5) * 26
output
[1] 11238513
[1] 292201338

The probability is 1 in 292,201,338. If you bought one ticket every second, day and night, you'd expect to wait over nine years for a jackpot.

Putting it in perspective. With a probability of about 3.4×10−9 per ticket, buying 100 tickets a week for 50 years (260,000 tickets) gives a chance of roughly 260,000/292,201,338≈0.0009 of ever winning the jackpot: less than 1 in 1,000. Chapter 4 (Example 4.5) works out what a ticket is worth on average, including the smaller prizes.

Example 3.11: Auditing a Drug Seizure ★ lecture example

Police seize 2,000 small bags of powder. Unknown to anyone, 100 of them are fakes (no controlled substance). The lab tests a random sample of 20 bags. What is the probability that the sample contains no fakes at all, so that the lab never discovers them?

Which case? The lab tests 20 different bags (no replacement), and the order of testing doesn't matter: case 3. A random sample makes every set of 20 bags equally likely, so count sets.

  • All possible samples: (200020).
  • Samples with no fakes: all 20 come from the 1,900 genuine bags, (190020).

Pr(no fakes in sample)=(190020)(200020)≈0.357.

R
choose(1900, 20) / choose(2000, 20)
output
[1] 0.356686

So about one time in three, a sample of 20 contains no fakes at all, even though 5% of the bags are fake. A clean sample does not prove the whole seizure is clean. A plot shows how the chance of missing every fake falls as the lab tests more bags:

R
k <- 1:100
p_miss <- choose(1900, k) / choose(2000, k)
ggplot(data.frame(k, p_miss), aes(k, p_miss)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "number of bags tested", y = "Pr(no fakes found)")

This calculation is the basis of the sampling plans forensic labs use to decide how many items to test (Exercise 5 asks how many are needed), and Chapter 4 turns it into the hypergeometric distribution.

Case 4: order doesn't matter, with replacement

The last case is the least obvious. A lab orders 10 reagent kits, and each kit can be one of 4 types (A, B, C, D). How many different orders are possible? Order doesn't matter (an order is just "how many of each type"), and types can repeat. An order might be 3 of A, 0 of B, 5 of C and 2 of D.

The trick, called stars and bars, is to draw each order as a row of 10 stars (the kits) separated by 4−1=3 bars into 4 compartments (the types). The order above is ⋆⋆⋆||⋆⋆⋆⋆⋆|⋆⋆ Three stars before the first bar (type A), none between the first and second bars (B), five between the second and third (C), and two after the third (D). Every order gives exactly one such row, and every row of 10 stars and 3 bars gives exactly one order. So we just count rows: 13 positions, of which we choose 3 for the bars, giving (133)=286 orders.

Theorem: Unordered Selections with Replacement (Stars and Bars)

The number of ways to choose k items from n distinct types, when order doesn't matter and types can repeat (equivalently, the number of ways to write k=x1+⋯+xn with each xi a whole number ≥0), is (n+k−1k)=(n+k−1n−1).

A selection is described completely by the counts (x1,…,xn) of each type, with x1+⋯+xn=k. Represent it as a row of k stars and n−1 bars: x1 stars, then a bar, then x2 stars, then a bar, and so on, ending with xn stars.

  • Every selection gives a row with exactly k stars and n−1 bars.
  • Every such row gives a selection: read off the numbers of stars between consecutive bars.

So selections and rows are in one-to-one correspondence, and we can count rows instead. A row has n+k−1 positions, and choosing which k of them hold stars (the rest hold bars) determines it completely. By case 3 there are (n+k−1k) ways; choosing the n−1 bar positions instead gives the same number. ◼∎

Watch Out: Counting Is Not the Same as Probability

Case 4 counts the possible unordered results, but those results are usually not equally likely, so you can't divide counts to get probabilities. Roll two dice and record the unordered result: by case 4 there are (6+2−12)=21 possible results ({1,1},{1,2},…). But {1,2} can happen two ways (1 then 2, or 2 then 1) while {1,1} can happen only one way, so Pr({1,2})=236 but Pr({1,1})=136. The equally likely outcomes are the 36 ordered pairs. When in doubt, count ordered outcomes. (In 1754 the great mathematician Jean d'Alembert made a closely related mistake, arguing that the chance of at least one head in two coin tosses is 2/3, because he treated three possible results as equally likely when they are not.)

The widget lists every selection for small cases, so you can see where all four formulas come from.

List every selection

Choose how many letters to pick from (n), how many to select (k), whether order matters, and whether letters can be reused. Every possible selection is listed, and the count is compared with the formula. Notice how each "order does not matter" list is a shorter version of the matching "order matters" list.

Check Yourself

The cases are different, so does it matter which analyst gets which case? Can one analyst get two of the cases?

Giving case 1 to Ana and case 2 to Ben differs from the reverse, so order matters; and each analyst gets at most one case, so no replacement: 8×7×6=336 ways.

order matters, without replacement

In how many different orders can 5 suspects be arranged in a line-up?

5 choices for the first position, then how many for the second?

5!=5×4×3×2×1=120.

A lab must choose 2 of its 5 analysts to review a case (order doesn't matter). How many different review panels are possible?

Ordered pairs: 5×4=20. How many times is each unordered pair counted in that 20?

(52)=5×42=10. In R: choose(5, 2).

A 4-digit PIN uses digits 0–9, and repeats are allowed. What is the probability that a random guess is right?

10×9×8×7=5040 counts PINs with no repeated digits. Can a PIN be 1111?

(104)=210 ignores order. Is 1234 the same PIN as 4321?

Each of 4 positions has 10 choices: 104=10,000 equally likely PINs.

A café sells 6 flavours of doughnut. How many different boxes of 2 doughnuts are possible, if a box can contain two of the same flavour and the order in the box doesn't matter?

This is case 4 with n=6 types and k=2 items: (n+k−1k).

(72)=21: the 15 boxes with two different flavours, (62), plus the 6 boxes with two of the same.

Think About It: Is It Really Equally Likely?

Counting only gives probabilities when the outcomes really are equally likely. For each claim, decide whether "equally likely" is a reasonable model: (a) each of the 10 digits is equally likely to be the last digit of a randomly chosen phone number; (b) each of the 104 PINs is equally likely to be someone's bank PIN; (c) a randomly chosen person is equally likely to be born on any day of the year.

(a) Reasonable: last digits are assigned with no preference. (b) Not at all: people choose 1234, 0000, birth years and dates far more than random strings; studies of leaked PINs find 1234 alone is used by around 1 in 10 people. An attacker predicts using that skewed distribution, not the uniform one. (c) Roughly, but not exactly: births vary by season and are less common on weekends and holidays (because of scheduled deliveries). The birthday problem's probability of 0.507 for 23 people is a slight underestimate for real people, because unequal birthdays make matches more likely.

Key Takeaways
  • With equally likely outcomes, Pr(A) is the number of outcomes in A divided by the total number of outcomes.
  • Ask two questions: does order matter? are repeats allowed? Then: nk; n!/(n−k)!; (nk); (n+k−1k).
  • Every formula comes from the multiplication rule, plus dividing out orderings that were counted more than once.
  • For "at least one" problems, count the complement. Coincidences are common: there are many more pairs than people.

3.5 Conditional probability and independence

Zooming in

Of the 2,201 people aboard the Titanic, 711 survived: Pr(survived)=711/2201≈0.32. But that number hides enormous differences. Suppose you learn that the person you picked was a woman. Your probability should change, because women were far more likely to be given places in the lifeboats. Learning something narrows the sample space to the outcomes consistent with what you learned. Try it.

Conditioning is zooming in: the Titanic

Each dot is one of the 2,201 people aboard the Titanic (R's Titanic data): filled dots survived, hollow dots did not. Pick a random person from the whole ship and the chance they survived is the fraction of filled dots. Now condition: choose a class, sex or age. Everyone outside your choice fades away, and the probability is recomputed among the people who remain. That is all a conditional probability is.

Among the 470 women, 344 survived, so the probability of survival given that the person was female is 344/470≈0.73. Notice how this was computed: restrict attention to the women, then take the fraction who survived. In a Venn diagram, the new information shrinks the sample space from the whole rectangle to the circle "female", and we ask what share of that circle lies inside "survived". Dividing both counts by 2,201 turns this into probabilities, and gives the general definition.

Definition: Conditional Probability

For events A and B with Pr(B)>0, the conditional probability of A given B is Pr(A∣B)=Pr(A∩B)Pr(B). It is the probability of A in a world where we know B has happened. The vertical bar is read "given".

Check it on the Titanic: Pr(survived∣female)=Pr(survived∩female)Pr(female)=344/2201470/2201=344470≈0.73. The 2,201s cancel: conditioning is just counting within the smaller group.

Rearranging the definition gives a rule for "and" that we'll use all the time.

Theorem: Multiplication Rule

For events A and B with Pr(B)>0, Pr(A∩B)=Pr(B)Pr(A∣B). More generally, for three events (with Pr(A1∩A2)>0), Pr(A1∩A2∩A3)=Pr(A1)×Pr(A2∣A1)×Pr(A3∣A1∩A2),Pr(A1∩A2∩A3)=Pr(A1)×Pr(A2∣A1)×Pr(A3∣A1∩A2), and so on for more events.

Multiply both sides of the definition by Pr(B). For three events, apply the two-event rule twice, first with B=A1∩A2: Pr(A1∩A2∩A3)=Pr(A1∩A2)×Pr(A3∣A1∩A2),Pr(A1∩A2∩A3)=Pr(A1∩A2)×Pr(A3∣A1∩A2), then to Pr(A1∩A2)=Pr(A1)Pr(A2∣A1). ◼∎

In words: the chance that both happen is the chance the first happens, times the chance the second happens given the first. Drawing two cards from a deck without replacement, the chance both are aces is 452×351: after the first ace, only 3 aces remain among 51 cards.

Example 3.12: Who Survived the Titanic? ★ lecture example

Using R's Titanic data, find the probability of survival given each class of travel, and given each sex. Then find Pr(female∣survived) and compare it with Pr(survived∣female).

prop.table(table, 1) divides each row of a table by its row total, which is exactly conditioning on the row; prop.table(table, 2) divides by column totals, conditioning on the column.

R
tt <- as.data.frame(Titanic)
by_class <- xtabs(Freq ~ Class + Survived, data = tt)
by_class
round(prop.table(by_class, 1), 3)     # Pr(survived | class): divide by row totals
by_sex <- xtabs(Freq ~ Sex + Survived, data = tt)
round(prop.table(by_sex, 1), 3)       # Pr(survived | sex)
round(prop.table(by_sex, 2), 3)       # Pr(sex | survived): divide by column totals
output
      Survived
Class   No Yes
  1st  122 203
  2nd  167 118
  3rd  528 178
  Crew 673 212
      Survived
Class     No   Yes
  1st  0.375 0.625
  2nd  0.586 0.414
  3rd  0.748 0.252
  Crew 0.760 0.240
        Survived
Sex         No   Yes
  Male   0.788 0.212
  Female 0.268 0.732
        Survived
Sex         No   Yes
  Male   0.915 0.516
  Female 0.085 0.484
R
rate <- prop.table(by_class, 1)[, "Yes"]
ggplot(data.frame(class = names(rate), rate), aes(class, rate)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 711 / 2201, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Pr(survived | class)")
  • Survival given class: 62% in first class, 41% in second, 25% in third, 24% among the crew. The dashed line is the overall rate, 32%: conditioning on class moves the probability a long way in both directions.
  • Survival given sex: 73% of females, 21% of males.
  • Pr(survived∣female)=344/470≈0.73, but Pr(female∣survived)=344/711≈0.48.

The last two are different questions with different answers. The first asks "of the women, what fraction survived?" (restrict to the 470 women); the second asks "of the survivors, what fraction were women?" (restrict to the 711 survivors). Same numerator, different group. Pr(A∣B) and Pr(B∣A) are not the same, and confusing them is the single most common error in probability. Section 3.6 shows how dangerous it can be.

Causal Inference: Conditioning Is Not Intervening

First-class passengers survived far more often than third-class passengers. Does that mean that buying a first-class ticket caused a better chance of survival? Partly, perhaps: first-class decks were closer to the lifeboats. But class was also tied up with sex and age (third class held many more families with children, for instance) and with where cabins were located.

Pr(survived∣first class) describes the people who happened to travel first class. The causal question, "what would happen to a person's chances if we moved them to first class?", is about an intervention, which statisticians write Pr(survived∣do(first class)). The two agree only when nothing else connects class and survival. Conditional probabilities describe the world as we find it; causal questions ask how it would change if we acted on it.

Reading a probability word problem

Most mistakes in probability happen before any calculation: in reading the question. A word problem hides its probabilities in everyday phrases, and the hardest part is deciding which phrase is a plain probability, which is an "and", and which is a "given". This algorithm works for almost every problem in the course.

Idea: Algorithm: From Words to Symbols

  1. Name the events. Give each yes/no feature a letter: D = "has the disease", + = "tests positive". Use complements for the opposite (Dc = "doesn't have the disease") rather than new letters.
  2. Translate every number. For each number in the question, ask: what fraction of what? The "of what" is the group you're restricted to. If it's everyone, it's a plain probability Pr(⋅). If it's a subgroup, it's a conditional probability, with the subgroup after the bar.
  3. Translate the question the same way.
  4. Choose the rule that connects what you have to what you want: complement, addition, multiplication, total probability or Bayes.
  5. Sanity check the answer: is it between 0 and 1? Is it bigger or smaller than you expected, and why?

The phrases below are clues to the translation. The most important one is that "of", "among", "if", "given that" and "for those who" all introduce the group after the bar.

phrase translation
"30% of patients have D" Pr(D)=0.3
"40% of smokers have D" / "if a person smokes, the chance of D is 40%" / "among smokers..." Pr(D∣smoker)=0.4
"10% of patients both smoke and have D" / "...are smokers with D" Pr(smoker∩D)=0.1
"of those with D, 25% smoke" Pr(smoker∣D)=0.25
"at least one", "either ... or" union, ∪
"neither", "none" complement of the union
"the test is 95% accurate for people who have D" (sensitivity) Pr(+∣D)=0.95
"a false-positive rate of 2%" Pr(+∣Dc)=0.02

Example 3.13: Translating a Word Problem ★ lecture example

In a city, 12% of adults were victims of a property crime last year. Among victims, 35% reported the crime to the police. Among non-victims, 1% filed a police report anyway (for example, for lost property later recovered). Of all the adults who filed a report, what fraction were genuine victims?

Translate every number into symbols, then solve.

Step 1, name the events. V = "was a victim", R = "filed a report". Then Vc = "not a victim".

Step 2, translate every number.

  • "12% of adults were victims": a fraction of all adults, so Pr(V)=0.12. (So Pr(Vc)=0.88.)
  • "Among victims, 35% reported": a fraction of victims, so it's conditional on V: Pr(R∣V)=0.35.
  • "Among non-victims, 1% filed a report": Pr(R∣Vc)=0.01.

Step 3, translate the question. "Of all the adults who filed a report, what fraction were victims?" The group is those who filed a report, so it goes after the bar: we want Pr(V∣R).

Notice that we were given Pr(R∣V) and are asked for Pr(V∣R): the question turns the conditional probability around. That is the signal for Bayes' theorem (Section 3.6).

Step 4, solve. It's easiest with natural frequencies. Imagine 10,000 adults:

  • 1,200 victims, of whom 35% report: 420 reports;
  • 8,800 non-victims, of whom 1% report: 88 reports.

So there are 420+88=508 reports, and 420 of them are from victims: Pr(V∣R)≈420508≈0.83.

Step 5, sanity check. About 83% of reports come from real victims, so about 17% don't, which is plausible: non-victims rarely report, but there are many more of them. Note how different this is from Pr(R∣V)=0.35.

The same reasoning as a picture. The 508 reports split into two very unequal sources:

R
ggplot(data.frame(source = c("genuine victims", "non-victims"), n = c(420, 88)),
       aes(x = "reports", y = n, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) + coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey40", "orange")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "reports per 10,000 adults", fill = NULL)

Check Yourself

Translate each statement. A forensic glass study found: "Of the fragments from vehicle windows, 30% had a refractive index above 1.52. Overall, 8% of fragments came from vehicle windows. 4% of all fragments both came from vehicle windows and had a high refractive index." Let V = "from a vehicle window" and H = "refractive index above 1.52".

"Of the fragments from vehicle windows" names the group you are restricted to. Does it go before or after the bar?

The group (vehicle windows) goes after the bar: Pr(H∣V)=0.3. It says nothing about fragments from other sources.

Pr(H∣V)=0.3

"Overall" means the group is all fragments. Is there any restriction?

No restriction: it's a plain probability, Pr(V)=0.08.

Pr(V)=0.08

"Of all fragments" means no restriction; "both ... and" means intersection.

Pr(V∩H)=0.04. (Careful: this can't be consistent with the first two statements, since Pr(V)Pr(H∣V)=0.08×0.3=0.024. A critical reader checks that the numbers in a problem agree with each other, and here one of them must be wrong.)

Pr(V∩H)=0.04

Independence

Sometimes learning that B happened tells us nothing about A: the probability stays the same.

Definition: Independent Events

Events A and B are independent if Pr(A∩B)=Pr(A)Pr(B). When Pr(B)>0 this is the same as Pr(A∣B)=Pr(A): knowing B happened doesn't change the probability of A. Events A1,…,An are (mutually) independent if, for every sub-collection of two or more of them, the probability that they all occur is the product of their probabilities.

Why are the two forms the same? If Pr(B)>0, dividing Pr(A∩B)=Pr(A)Pr(B) by Pr(B) gives Pr(A∩B)/Pr(B)=Pr(A), which says Pr(A∣B)=Pr(A); the steps reverse too.

For the Titanic, Pr(female)Pr(survived)=4702201×7112201≈0.069, but Pr(female∩survived)=3442201≈0.156. Not even close: sex and survival were strongly dependent.

In practice we usually assume independence because of how an experiment works (separate coin flips, separate patients, separate random draws with replacement), and then use the product rule to compute probabilities that would otherwise be impossible. Assuming independence is a modelling decision, and it deserves the same scepticism as any other assumption.

Watch Out: Independent Is Not the Same as Disjoint

Disjoint events are as dependent as events can be. If A and B are disjoint and both possible, then knowing A happened tells you for certain that B didn't: Pr(B∣A)=0≠Pr(B). In a Venn diagram, disjoint events don't overlap at all; independent events overlap by exactly the "right" amount, Pr(A)Pr(B).

Example 3.14: Independent Alarms?

In Example 3.6, detector A falsely alarmed on 3% of days, detector B on 4%, and both on 1%. Are the detectors' false alarms independent? What is Pr(B∣A), and what does it mean?

If they were independent, both would alarm on Pr(A)Pr(B)=0.03×0.04=0.0012 of days. In fact both alarm on 0.01 of days, more than 8 times as often. So they are not independent. Conditioning shows the strength of the connection: Pr(B∣A)=Pr(A∩B)Pr(A)=0.010.03≈0.33. On an ordinary day, B alarms with probability 0.04; on a day when A alarms, B alarms with probability 0.33. A false alarm from A makes one from B about eight times more likely, presumably because both are fooled by the same unusual traffic. Two detectors that fail together protect you less than two independent ones.

Example 3.15: The Chevalier De Méré's Dice ★ lecture example

De Méré believed these two bets were equally good:

  • Bet 1: at least one six in 4 rolls of a die;
  • Bet 2: at least one double six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice.

His reasoning: a six has chance 16 and there are 4 rolls, giving 46; a double six has chance 136 and there are 24 rolls, giving 2436=46. Yet, so the story goes, he lost money on the second bet. Find the correct probabilities.

What's wrong with de Méré's reasoning? It can't be right: by the same logic, 7 rolls would give a probability of 76>1. He added probabilities of events that are not disjoint (you can get a six on roll 1 and on roll 2), so the overlaps were counted more than once.

Use the complement and independence instead. For bet 1, "at least one six" is the complement of "no six in any of the 4 rolls". The rolls are independent and each misses a six with probability 56, so by the product rule Pr(at least one six)=1−(56)4≈1−0.4823=0.5177. For bet 2, each roll of the pair fails to give a double six with probability 3536: Pr(at least one double six)=1−(3536)24≈1−0.5086=0.4914.

R
1 - (5/6)^4
1 - (35/36)^24
output
[1] 0.5177469
[1] 0.4914039

Bet 1 wins slightly more than half the time, and bet 2 slightly less. De Méré was a sharp gambler: to notice a difference of less than 3 percentage points from his winnings, he must have played a great many times. The Law of Large Numbers at work.

A simulation of both bets shows how slowly the difference emerges, which is why de Méré needed so many games to notice it:

R
set.seed(1654)
n <- 20000
bet1 <- replicate(n, any(sample(1:6, 4, replace = TRUE) == 6))
bet2 <- replicate(n, any(sample(1:6, 24, replace = TRUE) == 6 & sample(1:6, 24, replace = TRUE) == 6))
d <- rbind(data.frame(play = 1:n, wins = cumsum(bet1) / (1:n), bet = "bet 1: one six in 4 rolls"),
           data.frame(play = 1:n, wins = cumsum(bet2) / (1:n), bet = "bet 2: double six in 24 rolls"))
ggplot(d, aes(play, wins, linetype = bet)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey60") +
  scale_x_log10() + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.3, 0.7)) +
  labs(x = "number of plays (log scale)", y = "fraction won so far", linetype = NULL)

In this run the lines part early, but that is partly luck: with a gap of under 3 percentage points, a run of a few hundred plays could easily show the bets the other way round, and it takes a few thousand plays before the difference is reliably clear. Detecting a small difference takes a lot of data, a theme Chapters 8 and 9 make precise.

Example 3.16: Why a DNA Profile Is So Rare

Forensic DNA profiles in the US record the variants a person carries at 20 standard locations (loci) on the genome, the CODIS core loci. Suppose that at each locus, the variants found at the crime scene occur in about 1 in 10 people, and that loci are independent of each other. What is the probability that a randomly chosen unrelated person matches at all 20 loci? What assumption is doing all the work?

With independence, the probabilities multiply: Pr(match at all 20 loci)=(110)20=10−20. That is one in a hundred billion billion, far smaller than one divided by the number of people who have ever lived.

Two assumptions are doing the work. The first is independence across loci, which is approximately true for unrelated people because the loci sit far apart on the genome. The second is that the chance of matching at each locus is about 1 in 10, which is true only for people unrelated to the true source. A brother inherited his DNA from the same parents, so at each locus his chance of carrying the same variants is much higher (roughly 1 in 4 or more), and his overall match probability is vastly larger than 10−20. That's why forensic reports state match probabilities for unrelated individuals, and why defence experts ask about relatives. (Real calculations also use the actual population frequencies of each variant, which differ between loci and populations; 1 in 10 is a simplification.)

Causal Inference: A Dependence Created by Looking

Two events can be independent in the population but dependent in your data, purely because of how the data were selected. Suppose two diseases, A and B, occur independently, and either one can put you in hospital. Among hospital patients, the diseases look negatively related: if a patient doesn't have A, something else (probably B) must have brought them in.

A variable caused by two others, like "in hospital" here, is called a collider. Conditioning on a collider (studying only hospital patients) creates a dependence between its causes. This is Berkson's paradox, described by the statistician Joseph Berkson in 1946. A simulation shows it clearly:

R
set.seed(46)
n <- 100000
A <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.10)                  # disease A: 10% of people
B <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.10)                  # disease B: 10%, independent of A
# admitted if ill and the illness is serious enough (50%), or for other reasons (2%)
hosp <- ((A == 1 | B == 1) & runif(n) < 0.5) | (runif(n) < 0.02)
# Pr(B | A) and Pr(B | not A), in everyone and among hospital patients
c(with_A = mean(B[A == 1]), without_A = mean(B[A == 0]))
c(with_A = mean(B[A == 1 & hosp]), without_A = mean(B[A == 0 & hosp]))
output
    with_A  without_A 
0.09671642 0.10058922 
    with_A  without_A 
0.09903661 0.73431199

In the whole population (first line), about 10% have disease B whether or not they have A. Among hospital patients (second line), only about 10% of those with A have B, but over 70% of those without A do. In hospital, the two diseases look strongly negatively related, though in reality they have nothing to do with each other. The same trap catches studies of only convicted defendants, only published papers, or only successful start-ups.

Interlude (Optional): Predicting the Next Word

A large language model, the technology behind modern AI chatbots, does one thing over and over: given the words so far, it assigns a probability to every possible next word, then picks one. In the language of this section, it computes a conditional probability for every possible word w: Pr(next word=w∣the words so far). And it estimates those conditional probabilities the way Section 3.1 estimated any probability: empirically, from how often each word followed similar text in its training data.

The idea is old. In 1948 Claude Shannon, founding information theory, generated English-like text by choosing each word according to how often it followed the previous word in a book: an empirical estimate of Pr(next word∣previous word). Here is Shannon's model, trained on a short made-up passage about a crime lab. Change the text, or paste in anything you like.

Predicting the next word

This is a tiny language model. It reads a training text and counts, for every word, which words came next. Its prediction for the next word is a conditional probability: Pr(next word = w | current word = x) = (times x was followed by w) ÷ (times x appeared). Type a word to see its predictions, or let the model write by repeatedly sampling a next word. You can replace the training text with anything you like.

Conditioning on only one previous word produces text that is locally plausible and globally nonsense. Modern models condition on thousands of previous words, and estimate the conditional probabilities with neural networks trained on enormous amounts of text. They still have to solve the problems you can see here: what to do about word combinations never seen in training (should their probability really be zero?), and how to choose a word: always the most likely one (dull and repetitive), or at random according to the probabilities (more varied, sometimes wrong). When a chatbot confidently states something false, it's because a plausible-sounding next word is not the same as a true one.

Why it matters: conditional probability, estimated from data, is the engine of modern AI.

Check Yourself

In a city, 40% of adults own a car and 25% own a bicycle. 10% own both.

What is the probability that a car owner also owns a bicycle?

Restrict to car owners: Pr(bike∣car)=Pr(bike and car)/Pr(car).

0.10/0.40=0.25.

Are owning a car and owning a bicycle independent in this city?

Compare Pr(bike∣car) with Pr(bike), or check whether Pr(car)Pr(bike)=Pr(both).

Pr(bike∣car)=0.25=Pr(bike); equivalently 0.4×0.25=0.10. Learning that someone owns a car tells you nothing about whether they own a bicycle.

Two security cameras independently fail on 2% of nights each. On what fraction of nights do both fail?

4% would be the chance of at least one failing (approximately). Both failing needs camera 1 and camera 2 to fail.

For independent events, Pr(both)=Pr(A)Pr(B).

Is 2% of 2% bigger or smaller than 2%?

0.02×0.02=0.0004, or 0.04% of nights. Redundant systems are reliable if their failures really are independent. A shared power supply would make them dependent.

Think About It: Which Way Round Is the Evidence?

A crime lab reports: "If the suspect is innocent, the probability of finding this many glass fragments on his clothing is 0.01." A newspaper headline says: "99% chance suspect is guilty, says lab." Explain, using the notation of this section, why the headline doesn't follow. What else would you need to know?

The lab reported Pr(evidence∣innocent)=0.01. The headline claims Pr(guilty∣evidence)=0.99, the conditional probability turned around: exactly the confusion of Example 3.12. To get from one to the other you need the probability of the evidence if he is guilty (perhaps not 1: guilty people don't always carry fragments), and how plausible his guilt was before the evidence: the prior. Section 3.6 shows how to combine them.

Key Takeaways

  • Pr(A∣B)=Pr(A∩B)/Pr(B): the probability of A after zooming in to the outcomes where B happened.
  • Multiplication rule Pr(A∩B)=Pr(B)Pr(A∣B).
  • In a word problem, ask of every number: what fraction of what? The "of what" goes after the bar.
  • A and B are independent if Pr(A∩B)=Pr(A)Pr(B). Disjoint events with positive probabilities are not independent.
  • Pr(A∣B)≠Pr(B∣A) in general.
  • Conditioning describes the world as found; causal questions ask about interventions. Conditioning on a collider creates false associations.

3.6 Thinking backwards: total probability and Bayes' theorem

From clues to causes

A detective arrives at a crime scene. She doesn't see the crime; she sees its effects: a footprint, a broken lock, a missing file. Her job is to reason backwards from the effects to the cause. A doctor does the same with symptoms, a mechanic with a strange noise, a scientist with an experiment's results.

Probability, so far, has gone forwards: if this person has the disease, how likely is a positive test? If this suspect is the thief, how likely is this footprint? Those forward probabilities are usually the ones we know, because we can study them: run the test on people known to be ill, measure the suspect's shoes. But the question we need answered goes backwards: given the positive test, how likely is the disease? Given the footprint, how likely is this suspect?

Two results connect the directions. The law of total probability says how likely a clue is overall, adding up over all the possible causes. Bayes' theorem then says what share of that total each cause is responsible for. Both are easiest to understand, and much harder to get wrong, if you start by counting.

Where do the clues come from? Total probability

Example 3.17: Where Do Lab Errors Come from? ★ lecture example

A crime lab sends DNA samples to three contract labs. Lab 1 processes 50% of the samples, lab 2 processes 30%, and lab 3 processes 20%. From audits, lab 1 makes an error on 1% of its samples, lab 2 on 2%, and lab 3 on 5%. (a) What fraction of all samples come back with an error? (b) A sample comes back with an error. What is the probability it was processed by lab 3?

Translate. Let L1,L2,L3 be the events that a sample went to each lab, and E that it comes back with an error. The question gives Pr(L1)=0.5, Pr(L2)=0.3, Pr(L3)=0.2, and, because "lab 1 makes an error on 1% of its samples" restricts to lab 1, Pr(E∣L1)=0.01, Pr(E∣L2)=0.02, Pr(E∣L3)=0.05. We want (a) Pr(E) and (b) Pr(L3∣E).

Count first. Imagine 1,000 samples.

lab samples error rate errors
1 500 1% 5
2 300 2% 6
3 200 5% 10
total 1,000 21

(a) Altogether there are 5+6+10=21 errors in 1,000 samples, so Pr(E)=21/1000=0.021. We found the overall error rate by adding up the errors from each source.

(b) Now look only at the 21 samples with errors. Ten of them came from lab 3, so Pr(L3∣E)=1021≈0.48. Lab 3 handles only 20% of the samples, but nearly half of the errors.

The same calculation in symbols. The 5, 6 and 10 were each "number of samples × error rate", that is, 1000×Pr(Li)×Pr(E∣Li). So the total was Pr(E)=Pr(E∣L1)Pr(L1)+Pr(E∣L2)Pr(L2)+Pr(E∣L3)Pr(L3)=0.01×0.5+0.02×0.3+0.05×0.2=0.005+0.006+0.010=0.021,Pr(E)=Pr(E∣L1)Pr(L1)+Pr(E∣L2)Pr(L2)+Pr(E∣L3)Pr(L3)=0.01×0.5+0.02×0.3+0.05×0.2=0.005+0.006+0.010=0.021, and the share from lab 3 was Pr(L3∣E)=Pr(E∣L3)Pr(L3)Pr(E)=0.0100.021≈0.48. These are the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem. You've just used both, without needing either formula.

Play with the same calculation below. Each square is one case. Step 1 is the law of total probability (count all the dark squares); step 2 is Bayes' theorem (zoom in on the dark squares and ask where they came from).

1,000 cases: where do the events come from?

Each small square is one of 1,000 cases, coloured by which group it belongs to. Dark squares with a dot are the cases where the event happened. Step 1 (law of total probability): count all the dark squares, group by group. Step 2 (Bayes' theorem): press look only at the event to zoom in on the dark squares and ask which group they came from. Change the rates and watch both answers move.

Now the general statement. The idea is that the possible causes B1,…,Bk split the sample space into pieces, like the labs above, and every outcome lies in exactly one piece. Such a collection is called a partition of S.

Theorem: Law of Total Probability

Suppose the events B1,B2,…,Bk are disjoint, have positive probability, and between them cover the whole sample space (exactly one of them happens). Then for any event A, Pr(A)=Pr(A∣B1)Pr(B1)+Pr(A∣B2)Pr(B2)+⋯+Pr(A∣Bk)Pr(Bk). In words: the overall probability of A is a weighted average of its probabilities within each piece, weighted by how big each piece is.

Because exactly one Bi happens, A splits into the disjoint pieces A∩B1,…,A∩Bk ("A and the cause was B1", and so on). By axiom 3, Pr(A)=Pr(A∩B1)+⋯+Pr(A∩Bk). Apply the multiplication rule to each term: Pr(A∩Bi)=Pr(A∣Bi)Pr(Bi). ◼∎

The most common partition has just two pieces, B and Bc: Pr(A)=Pr(A∣B)Pr(B)+Pr(A∣Bc)Pr(Bc). Why is it intuitive? It's how you'd compute an overall pass rate for a course with two sections: each section's pass rate, weighted by the share of students in it. If one section has 90% passing and holds a quarter of the students, and the other has 70% passing, the overall rate is 0.9×0.25+0.7×0.75=0.75. The overall rate must lie between the section rates, and it's closer to the bigger section's.

Reasoning backwards: Bayes' theorem

Here is the classic example, in which most doctors get it wrong. We'll do it with frequencies first, and only then with the formula.

Example 3.18: A Positive Mammogram ★ lecture example

In a study by Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues (published in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2007), 160 gynaecologists were given this information about mammography screening in their region:

  • the probability that a woman has breast cancer is 1% (the prevalence);
  • if she has breast cancer, the probability that the mammogram is positive is 90% (the sensitivity);
  • if she doesn't, the probability that it is nevertheless positive is 9% (the false-positive rate).

A woman's mammogram is positive. What is the probability she actually has breast cancer? Make a guess before reading on.

Translate. Write C for "has cancer" and + for "positive test". Then Pr(C)=0.01 (all women), Pr(+∣C)=0.9 ("if she has cancer"), and Pr(+∣Cc)=0.09 ("if she doesn't"). The question asks for Pr(C∣+) ("given a positive"): the reverse of what we know.

Count first: natural frequencies. Imagine 1,000 women having a mammogram.

Ten have cancer, and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 without cancer, 9% (about 89) also test positive. So there are 9+89=98 positive tests, of which only 9 come from women with cancer: Pr(C∣+)≈998≈0.09.

Only about 9%. The disease is rare, so even a small false-positive rate applied to the large healthy majority produces far more false alarms (89) than true cases (9).

The same calculation in symbols. The 98 positives came from two sources, so the law of total probability gives Pr(+)=Pr(+∣C)Pr(C)+Pr(+∣Cc)Pr(Cc)=0.9×0.01+0.09×0.99=0.009+0.0891=0.0981,Pr(+)=Pr(+∣C)Pr(C)+Pr(+∣Cc)Pr(Cc)=0.9×0.01+0.09×0.99=0.009+0.0891=0.0981, and the share of those that come from women with cancer is Pr(C∣+)=Pr(+∣C)Pr(C)Pr(+)=0.0090.0981≈0.092.

In the study, only 21% of the gynaecologists chose the right answer (about 1 in 10); nearly half chose 90%, confusing Pr(+∣C) with Pr(C∣+), and 13% chose 81%, another answer far too high.
